content: Malic acid is an organic dicarboxylic acid with a tart flavor, commonly found in sour or tart foods. Its salts and esters are referred to as malates. The malate anion serves as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, alongside fumarate. Additionally, malate can be synthesized from pyruvate through anaplerotic reactions. Malic acid was first isolated in 1785 by Carl Wilhelm Scheele from apple juice. In 1787, Antoine Lavoisier proposed the name acide malique, derived from the Latin word for apple, malum. Biochemically, malate is a significant compound. In nature, malic acid exists exclusively as the (-)-malic acid enantiomer. During the C4 carbon fixation process in plants, malate acts as a source of carbon dioxide for the Calvin cycle. Within the citric acid cycle, (S)-malate is formed by the addition of a hydroxyl group to the si face of fumarate. It can also be synthesized from pyruvate via anaplerotic reactions. The enzyme malate dehydrogenase facilitates the reversible conversion of malate to oxaloacetate, utilizing NAD as a cofactor. In plants, malate is produced from starch in the guard cells of leaves. An accumulation of malate reduces water potential, causing water to flow into the guard cells, which can lead to the opening of stomata. However, this process does not always guarantee stomatal opening. Malic acid is responsible for the sour taste of green apples. In winemaking, it contributes to the tartness of wine, although its concentration decreases as the fruit ripens. The process of malolactic fermentation converts malic acid into lactic acid, which has a milder taste. As a food additive, malic acid is identified by the E number E296. It is the primary source of the intense tartness in extreme candies such as Mega Warheads. It is also used in sour candies like Jolly Ranchers, SweeTarts, and Jimmy Johns Salt & Vinegar potato chips, either alone or as a substitute for citric acid. Some of these products carry warnings about potential mouth irritation from excessive consumption. Chemically, malic acid played a pivotal role in the discovery of the Walden inversion and the Walden cycle. In this cycle, (-)-malic acid is first converted into (+)-chlorosuccinic acid using phosphorus pentachloride. Treatment with wet silver oxide transforms this compound into (+)-malic acid, which can then react with phosphorus pentachloride to regenerate (-)-chlorosuccinic acid. The cycle is completed when silver oxide converts this compound back to (-)-malic acid. Additionally, the self-condensation of malic acid with fuming sulfuric acid produces the pyrone compound known as coumalic acid.
